title: The Song of the Reed
originalText: بشنو از نی چون حکایت می‌کند
در نفیرم مرد و زن نالیده‌اند
translation: Listen to the reed, how it tells its tale,
complaining, ever since, of being torn from the reed bed.
"Since they cut me from the marsh where I grew,
my cry has made every man and woman weep.
I want a breast torn open by parting,
so I can lay this longing bare.
Whoever is left far from their root
keeps searching for the day they were whole again."
In every gathering I sang my grief,
kept company with the joyful and the broken alike.
Each believed themselves my friend,
but none went looking for the secret inside me.
translator: Rendered for Golshan Raz, after the Persian
note: The Masnavi's six books open with this one image: a reed flute, cut from its bed and carved with holes, that can only make music because it grieves. Rumi's readers have always heard the reed as the soul itself, exiled into a body and singing of the union it remembers. Reynold A. Nicholson's 1898 English translation remains the standard scholarly rendering of the full Masnavi; the lines here are a new setting of its opening couplets for this collection.

title: Dance of the Moth
translation: The moth does not love the candle for its light.
It loves the candle for the ending it offers.
Circle after circle, closer, closer —
any fool can tell you this is not wisdom.
But ask the flame what it thinks of wisdom,
ask the ash what it thinks of caution.
I have stopped explaining myself to the lamp-tenders.
Let them keep their oil. I am going in.
translator: Rendered for Golshan Raz, after the Persian
note: The moth and the candle (parvāneh o sham') is one of the oldest images in Persian mystical verse, older than Rumi himself, used to picture a love that consumes the lover entirely — self-forgetting (fana) as the only honest response to the sight of God. Rumi returns to it across the Divan-e Shams, the vast, unruly collection of odes he composed in the name of his teacher and beloved, Shams-e Tabrizi.

title: What the Tavern-Keeper Knows
translation: Come in, the tavern-keeper says, we have no news here
of who is virtuous and who has failed.
We only ask one thing at the door:
did the wine reach you, or did you only watch it poured?
The scholars debate the shape of the cup for forty years.
The drunk was already home before they finished the first argument.
I am not telling you to abandon your reason.
I am telling you reason was never going to get you in.
translator: Rendered for Golshan Raz, after the Persian
note: Wine in Persian mystical poetry is rarely only wine. The tavern (kharabat) becomes a counter-mosque where rank and reputation dissolve, and drunkenness (mastī) stands for a knowledge that arrives through surrender rather than argument — a favorite provocation of Rumi's toward the jurists and theologians of his own former profession.

title: Turning
translation: I put the world down like a coat at the door
and turned. Not toward anything. Not away from anything.
My right hand opened to what descends.
My left hand opened to what I could finally let go of.
Somewhere in the turning the dancer disappeared
and only the turning was left, and that was enough,
that was the whole of the sermon I came here to give you:
stop watching the edge of the circle. Stand in the middle. Spin.
translator: Rendered for Golshan Raz, after the Persian
note: The whirling of the sema ceremony, formalized by Rumi's followers into the Mevlevi order after his death, is a devotional practice, not a performance: one hand raised to receive grace, the other lowered to pass it on to the earth. The image of the still center around which everything turns runs through Rumi's poetry as a figure for the unmoving divine at the heart of a changing world.

title: The Saqi's Cup
originalText: الا یا أیها الساقی أدر کأساً و ناولها
که عشق آسان نمود اول ولی افتاد مشکل‌ها
translation: Rise, cup-bearer, and bring the wine around —
love looked simple only from a distance.
I have counted every promise the beloved never kept
and still I set a place for them at my table.
The perfume that the morning wind carries from her hair
has cost this city a hundred restless hearts.
Dye your prayer-mat with wine if the old master tells you to —
the traveler on this road does not question the stations.
What do the dark night, the fear of the wave, this whirling storm know
of us, who once stood on the light shore with nothing to carry?
translator: Rendered for Golshan Raz, after the Persian
note: This is the ghazal that opens most editions of Hafez's Divan, and by tradition the first poem a reader meets when they consult it for fal-e Hafez — the practice of asking Hafez a question and letting the book's answer fall open at random. Its famous line about the night, the wave, and the whirlpool has been read equally as a sailor's memory and as a soul's account of being cast into the world far from God.

title: The Rose and the Nightingale
translation: The nightingale has loved the rose since before either of us was born,
and still each spring he sings as if it were the first garden.
She only opens for a matter of days.
He has a whole year of silence to compose the next song in.
Do not pity him his short-lived beloved.
Pity the ones who loved something that could not close and be gone.
A love with an ending sharpens every petal.
I have heard nightingales grieving over roses
that were, by any fair account, only thorns by autumn —
and I understood, finally, that he was never singing to the rose.
translator: Rendered for Golshan Raz, after the Persian
note: Gol-o-bolbol, the rose and the nightingale, is the great romantic pairing of the Persian garden tradition, appearing on carpets and manuscript margins as often as in verse. Hafez inherited the image from earlier poets but is famous for turning its sweetness sideways — using the doomed romance to talk about impermanence, and about a love aimed past its stated object toward the divine.

title: The Tavern of Ruin
translation: The preacher who shouts loudest against the tavern
is, by the accounts I've heard, its most faithful customer after dark.
I do not say this to shame him.
I say it because his secret and mine are the same secret.
We are all trying to get drunk enough on something
to survive the sober accounting of ourselves the world demands.
Go, then, to whichever ruin lets you tell the truth —
the mosque, the tavern, the empty road at 3 a.m.
God was never particular about the address.
God was only ever waiting to hear you stop performing.
translator: Rendered for Golshan Raz, after the Persian
note: Hafez writes often in the voice of the rend — a knowing, unashamed rogue who prefers the honest sinner to the performing saint. The kharabat, a ruined tavern outside the boundaries of respectable town life, becomes a favorite stage for this persona: a place where hypocrisy has no cover left to hide behind.

title: Morning in the Bowl of Night
translation: Awake! for Morning in the Bowl of Night
Has flung the Stone that puts the Stars to Flight:
And Lo! the Hunter of the East has caught
The Sultán's Turret in a Noose of Light.
note: The opening quatrain of FitzGerald's Rubáiyát, first published anonymously in 1859 and largely ignored until Dante Gabriel Rossetti and the Pre-Raphaelites found a discarded penny copy on a bookseller's cart. FitzGerald's is a famously free translation, weaving together many separate ruba'iyat attributed to Khayyam into a single day's arc from dawn to wine-dark evening — a poetic sequence more than a literal rendering.

title: The Bird of Time
translation: Come, fill the Cup, and in the Fire of Spring
Your Winter-garment of Repentance fling:
The Bird of Time has but a little way
To flutter—and the Bird is on the Wing.
note: Khayyam was a mathematician and astronomer who reformed the Persian solar calendar before he was, to English readers, a poet at all. Whether his quatrains are a skeptic's carpe diem or a Sufi's coded intoxication with the divine has been argued since FitzGerald's own century; the ambiguity is very likely the point.

title: A Book of Verse
translation: Here with a Loaf of Bread beneath the Bough,
A Flask of Wine, a Book of Verse—and Thou
Beside me singing in the Wilderness—
And Wilderness is Paradise enow.
note: Perhaps the most quoted quatrain in the English-language Rubáiyát, and the one most often lifted onto wedding invitations and garden gates. It compresses Khayyam's whole ethic into four lines: paradise is not a promised elsewhere but whatever bare ground you are standing on, made sufficient by bread, wine, verse, and company.

title: The Moving Finger
translation: The Moving Finger writes; and, having writ,
Moves on: nor all your Piety nor Wit
Shall lure it back to cancel half a Line,
Nor all your Tears wash out a Word of it.
note: FitzGerald revised his Rubáiyát across five editions between 1859 and 1889, and this quatrain — on the irreversibility of what has already been lived — belongs to the later, more widely printed text. It has outgrown Khayyam almost entirely to become a stand-alone English proverb about time.

title: Children of One Essence
originalText: که در آفرینش ز یک گوهرند
چو عضوی به درد آورد روزگار
translation: The children of Adam are limbs of one body,
cut, all of them, from a single essence.
When the days bring pain to one limb,
the rest cannot lie still in comfort.
You, who feel nothing at another's suffering,
do not deserve to be called by the name of a human being.
translator: Rendered for Golshan Raz, after the Persian
note: These six lines from the first chapter of the Golestan are perhaps the most quoted couplet in Persian ethical literature; a tapestry bearing them, gifted by Iran, hangs at the entrance to the United Nations headquarters in New York. Sa'di composed the Golestan in 1258, weaving verse through prose anecdotes drawn from a life of extensive travel — a form intended, unusually for its time, to be both moral instruction and genuinely pleasant reading.

title: The Rose That Fades, the Book That Stays
translation: A friend once brought me roses for my room
and I thought: by Friday these will be compost.
So I built a garden that does not answer to weather —
paper, ink, a few hundred sentences bound at the spine.
The wind cannot enter here and take a single petal.
Winter has no authority over this particular spring.
Six hundred years on, you are standing in it.
Tell me now which garden was the more lasting gift.
translator: Rendered for Golshan Raz, after the tradition of the Golestan's preface
note: Sa'di explains the title of his book in its own preface: a companion offered him fresh roses, and rather than watch the gift wilt within days, Sa'di resolved to make a rose garden that autumn could not touch — a garden of words. It is one of Persian literature's most self-aware openings, a book explaining, in effect, why it needed to exist at all.

title: The Valley of the Quest
collection: Mantiq al-Tayr (The Conference of the Birds)
translation: The hoopoe told them: the first valley has no map.
You will not be given a reason before you are asked to leave everything.
Some birds turned back at the border, citing the cold.
Some turned back citing the heat. Some simply forgot why they had come.
Those who went on lost, in this order:
their certainty, their comfort, their good opinion of themselves —
and found, in the place where those things had been standing,
a small clear space exactly the size of a single next step.
translator: Rendered for Golshan Raz, after the Persian
note: Attar's Mantiq al-Tayr sends the birds of the world on a pilgrimage across seven valleys — Quest, Love, Insight into Mystery, Detachment, Unity, Bewilderment, and Poverty and Nothingness — in search of their king, the mythical Simorgh. Led by the hoopoe, familiar to Persian readers as King Solomon's messenger bird, the flock thins at every valley until only thirty birds complete the journey.

title: Thirty Birds
collection: Mantiq al-Tayr (The Conference of the Birds)
translation: Thirty birds arrived, starving, at the mountain
where the Simorgh was said to hold court above the clouds.
The gate was a lake. They looked in, expecting a king,
and saw thirty exhausted, travel-ruined birds looking back.
For a long moment no one understood the joke God had made of the journey —
then all thirty began, at once, to laugh and weep in the same breath.
Si morgh, thirty birds: that was the name of what they had come so far to find.
It had been flying inside the flock the entire time.
translator: Rendered for Golshan Raz, after the Persian
note: The poem's ending turns on a pun no translation can fully carry: si morgh means 'thirty birds' in Persian, and simorgh names the fabled king-bird they have crossed seven valleys to find. Only thirty birds survive the journey, and what they find at its end is themselves, reflected — one of world literature's most compact statements of Sufi unity (tawhid), in which the seeker and the sought turn out to be a single reality.

title: The Valley of Bewilderment
collection: Mantiq al-Tayr (The Conference of the Birds)
translation: In the sixth valley even the compass stops pretending to know north.
You came here as someone who had answers, or who was at least
collecting better questions. Neither survives this air.
A bird asked the hoopoe: how will I know I have arrived?
The hoopoe said, you will stop asking that question.
Not because you found the answer.
Because you finally understood which of you was doing the asking.
translator: Rendered for Golshan Raz, after the Persian
note: Bewilderment (hayrat) is the sixth of the seven valleys, placed deliberately after Unity rather than before it: Attar insists the traveler must first taste oneness with the divine before the deeper, more disorienting bewilderment of realizing how little the self can claim to understand about that oneness.

title: The Secret Rose Garden
translation: A traveler from Herat sent seventeen questions east to Tabriz,
the kind that keep a serious person awake past the call to prayer.
What is the wayfarer? What is the wine that has no cask?
What does it mean that the world is His face, and He no face at all?
Shabistari answered each one in verse, over a single sitting,
as though the questions had been waiting inside him, already ripe.
A rose garden, he called the answers, and a secret —
not because the truth is hidden, but because it is standing in full sun
and you keep asking directions to a shaded, more difficult place.
translator: Rendered for Golshan Raz, after the Persian
note: In 1311, a Sufi traveling from Herat sent Mahmud Shabistari, then a young theologian in Tabriz, a list of seventeen technical questions on the nature of the mystic path. Shabistari is said to have composed his answers — the roughly one thousand couplets of the Gulshan-i Raz — in a single night. It became one of the most copied and commented-upon handbooks of Persian Sufi doctrine, still read as a compact summary of the whole path.

title: A Single Point
translation: Draw a point. Now spin it fast enough
and it will show you a perfect circle where no circle exists —
only ever the one point, moving, mistaken for many.
This is what the world is doing in front of you right now.
Multiplicity is only oneness, in a hurry, seen by a slow eye.
Stop the spinning for one honest moment
and count again how many things are actually out there.
translator: Rendered for Golshan Raz, after the Persian
note: Shabistari builds much of the Gulshan-i Raz on this kind of compressed geometric image: unity (tawhid) demonstrated not as an article of faith to be accepted but as something close to a proof, offered to a reader trained, like most of his original audience, in logic and cosmology as much as devotion.

title: What the Wayfarer Asked
translation: He asked: what is the self that must be lost along this road?
I told him: the self is the only lantern you were given
to find your way to the place where lanterns are no longer needed.
Do not smash it at the door out of impatience.
Carry it all the way in, and set it down only when the room is already lit.
That is the whole difficulty of the path, and the whole of its mercy:
you are not asked to arrive empty-handed, only willing to put the lamp down.
translator: Rendered for Golshan Raz, after the Persian
note: The Gulshan-i Raz is structured as a series of direct answers to a traveler's questions on Sufi terminology and practice — what is the self, what is the heart, what is the meaning of intoxication and sobriety on the path. Shabistari's habit of answering abstraction with a concrete, almost domestic image, as here, is much of why the poem became a teaching text rather than staying a private exchange of letters.
